The central question is when this assumption catastrophically fails, and why it fails in predictable ways when the fine-tuning objectives are heterogeneous—e.g., merging a model fine-tuned with SFT cross-entropy on instruction data with one fine-tuned via RLHF PPO on preference data, or merging a code specialist trained on execution feedback with a math specialist trained on chain-of-thought supervision. What a beginner misses is that the problem is not primarily about data distribution distance—it's about curvature alignment: two models can be trained on completely different domains but merge cleanly if their Hessians share eigenspace structure, while two models trained on superficially similar data can produce total loss landscape collapse if their optimization trajectories carved out minima with incompatible curvature orientations. The expert worry is that standard diagnostics (cosine similarity of task vectors, parameter-space distance) are blind to this curvature mismatch, so practitioners declare a merge "safe" based on surface-level metrics while the merged model sits in a high-loss saddle that evaluations on either constituent task will not immediately reveal—only held-out compositional tasks expose the damage.

Sign information alone is theoretically insufficient for identifying suppression coordinates, and PPO's gradient structure explains precisely why: PPO updates are computed as clipped surrogate gradients weighted by advantage estimates, meaning the sign of a parameter update reflects whether the advantage was positive or negative at the sampled token sequence, not whether the parameter encodes a behavioral constraint—a suppression coordinate that inhibits harmful outputs will have received negative advantage signal (the behavior was penalized) and thus a task vector entry pointing away from the pre-trained value, but so will any parameter that was simply overfit to a downvoted response for entirely unrelated stylistic reasons. The fundamental problem is that PPO's clipping mechanism (ε=0.1 or 0.2 in standard configurations) creates magnitude compression independent of functional importance: parameters encoding strong behavioral constraints are updated repeatedly across many batches but each individual update is clipped, producing a low-magnitude task vector entry that has the same sign profile as a parameter that received a single weak gradient signal—sign cannot distinguish accumulated-but-clipped suppression from incidental-and-weak noise. Rafailov et al.'s DPO analysis (2023) offers a partial counterargument: in DPO-trained models (which avoid PPO's clipping entirely), the implicit reward structure means suppression coordinates do tend to cluster in consistent sign directions across the full dataset, making sign patterns somewhat more informative—but this advantage disappears under PPO because the on-policy sampling introduces high variance in which suppression-relevant sequences even appear in the gradient computation. What sign patterns can reliably identify is inter-model consensus on behavioral direction: if you have multiple RLHF-trained models from the same base and their task vectors agree in sign on a low-magnitude parameter, that consensus is strong evidence the parameter is functionally constrained rather than noisy, which is exactly the intuition behind TIES's sign election step—but TIES applies this to resolve conflicts between models, not to protect low-magnitude entries from trimming, so the mechanism exists but is not wired to the right decision point. The rescue requires a two-pass procedure: first perform sign-consensus analysis across an ensemble of RLHF variants to identify low-magnitude parameters with high cross-model sign agreement, then exempt those parameters from trimming regardless of magnitude—a method that approximates reward-model access by using the population of RLHF outcomes as a proxy for the underlying preference geometry, at the cost of requiring multiple fine-tuned checkpoints rather than a single model pair.

DPO-SFT merges and PPO-SFT merges produce qualitatively distinct interference signatures localized to different architectural components, and the difference is traceable to how each training objective propagates gradients through the transformer stack. DPO's contrastive loss operates directly on log-probability differences between chosen and rejected completions, which means its gradients are densest in the early-to-mid attention layers (layers 4–16 in a 32-layer model like Llama-2-7B)—specifically the Q and K projection matrices where the model learns to differentially attend to preference-relevant token positions—producing task vectors with high-magnitude, high-sign-consistency entries concentrated in attention heads responsible for pragmatic interpretation of instructions. PPO by contrast propagates reward signal through a value network and then back through the policy via advantage-weighted likelihood, which diffuses gradient energy more broadly but with particular concentration in late MLP layers (layers 24–32) where token-level value predictions interact with the residual stream—this is consistent with Anthropic's interpretability findings on refusal mechanisms and with the observation that PPO-trained models like Llama-2-Chat show dramatic activation pattern changes in final-layer MLPs compared to their SFT baseline while DPO models like Zephyr-7B-β show more distributed changes centered on mid-layer attention. When you merge DPO+SFT, the interference is attention-subspace competitive: both models have dense task vectors in Q/K projections (SFT from learning instruction-following attention patterns, DPO from learning preference-discriminating attention patterns), producing high cosine similarity but destructive sign conflicts in exactly the heads that matter most for behavioral control, which manifests as merged models that attend correctly to instruction structure but lose the fine-grained preference sensitivity. PPO+SFT interference is instead MLP-residual-stream disruptive: the SFT model's MLP task vectors are relatively low-magnitude in late layers (SFT doesn't strongly reshape final-layer MLPs), so the PPO task vector's high-magnitude late-layer entries dominate the merge and push the residual stream into a high-curvature region the SFT model never visited, causing catastrophic forgetting of SFT-learned output formatting and instruction-following conventions that lived in those late MLPs. Practical confirmation comes from MergeKit practitioners and Goddard et al. (2024) noting that DPO merges require lower merge coefficients on attention weight groups (α≈0.3–0.4 for Q/K vs. α≈0.5–0.6 for MLPs) to avoid preference sensitivity collapse, while PPO merges require the inverse weighting—a layer-type-dependent α schedule that no standard merge toolkit exposes as a first-class parameter.

Activation-space merging partially sidesteps weight-space interference but trades one failure mode for another: by interpolating hidden states on a calibration set rather than parameters directly, you avoid the destructive sign conflicts in Q/K projections and the MLP residual-stream collisions, because you're operating on the outputs of those computations rather than the matrices themselves—but this only works for the specific input distribution covered by the calibration set, and the merged "model" is no longer a deployable weight matrix but a inference-time intervention that requires running both models forward on every token. The most developed instantiation of this idea is representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023), which identifies behavioral directions in activation space via contrastive pairs and steers hidden states at inference time—effectively a merge in activation space for a single behavioral dimension—and it demonstrably avoids the Q/K interference problem because it operates post-attention, injecting directly into the residual stream at chosen layers without touching weight matrices. However, representation engineering as a merge primitive hits a compositionality ceiling: Zou et al. and subsequent work (Rhinehart et al., 2024 on activation addition failures) show that adding more than 2–3 steering vectors simultaneously produces interference in activation space that mirrors the weight-space interference problem—the residual stream has finite capacity and simultaneous injections from DPO-derived and PPO-derived steering vectors compete for the same residual stream bandwidth, particularly at layers 14–20 where both objectives happen to have dense activation signatures. The deeper issue is that activation-space interpolation is only well-defined for a fixed forward pass graph: the calibration set determines which activation trajectories get interpolated, but transformer hidden states are input-dependent in ways that weight matrices are not—a merge coefficient α that produces coherent hidden states on the calibration distribution will produce incoherent interpolations on out-of-distribution inputs because the two models' activation geometries diverge in input-dependent ways that a static α cannot track. What this implies for representation engineering as a merge primitive is that it's genuinely viable for single-axis behavioral adjustment (toxicity reduction, refusal calibration, persona consistency) where one model provides a directional correction to another, but it fails as a general merge strategy for heterogeneous fine-tuning objectives because it requires solving the same interference problem in a higher-dimensional, input-dependent space without the compensating benefit of producing a deployable artifact—you get the costs of both weight-space and activation-space methods without the full benefits of either.

The input-conditioned routing function does reduce to MoE in the limit but the conceptual journey reveals a meaningful intermediate regime that practitioners are actively collapsing prematurely. If you parameterize α as a function of the current hidden state h—say, α(h) = σ(W_r · h) where W_r is a learned routing matrix—and train this on a calibration objective that rewards coherent output from the interpolated activations, you have exactly the per-token soft routing of a MoE layer, with the two "experts" being the full forward passes of the two merged models; Jacobs et al.'s original MoE formulation (1991) and the modern transformer instantiation in Shazeer et al. (2017) are structurally identical to this setup when α is allowed to be discrete. The meaningful distinction that exists before full reduction is in the routing input: standard MoE routers condition on the current token's hidden state within a single model's forward pass, while an input-conditioned merge router would ideally condition on the divergence between the two models' hidden states at that layer—routing to the model whose activation geometry is more confident or lower-entropy for the current input, which is a fundamentally different signal than either model's hidden state alone and cannot be computed without running both models forward. Raposo et al.'s mixture-of-depths work (2024) and the broader MoE routing literature show that routers trained on hidden states from a single model fail to generalize their routing decisions to inputs that shift the activation distribution, which is precisely the OOD failure mode we started with—so a router conditioned on the gap between models rather than a single model's representation would have better-grounded routing signal but at 2× inference cost. The practical reduction to MoE happens when you distill the two-model system into a single model with shared lower layers and divergent expert layers, which is exactly the recipe used in model merging via MoE conversion (Komatsuzaki et al., 2022; also the "Frankenmerge" → MoE pipeline in MergeKit)—but this distillation step throws away the interpolation interpretation entirely, replacing continuous α with discrete expert selection and losing the ability to represent genuinely intermediate behaviors that neither expert alone would produce. The residual meaningful distinction is therefore: interpolation captures convex combinations of behaviors that may not exist in either constituent model (a model that is 40% DPO-aligned and 60% SFT-fluent in a way neither alone achieves), while MoE routing selects among discrete behaviors and can only produce convex combinations implicitly through token-level mixing across a sequence—a distinction that matters enormously for tasks requiring sustained intermediate behavioral states rather than token-by-token switching.
